entry.title: Type a classifier straight into the trainer

link.title: Type a classifier straight into the trainer

entry.content:
The Intelligence Trainer has always worked from whatever is in front of you. You find a tag, an author, or a phrase on a story, and you train it from there. That’s fine when the story is right there, but someone on the forum asked a fair question: what if you already know what you want? You’d like every title with “sponsored” in it hidden across all of your sites, and you’d rather not wait for one to show up first. There was no way to do that. Now there is.

Add a classifier

Open the Intelligence Trainer and switch to Manage Training. There’s a new panel at the top. Pick what to match (title, author, tag, text, or URL), type the phrase, choose where it applies, pick Like, Dislike, or Hide, and press Add. It saves right away, the new classifier lights up in its section below, and the field clears so you can type the next one.

Enter in the phrase field does the same thing as Add, and the little ↵ on the button reminds you while you type. Your choices stick between adds, so putting a dozen tags into the same folder is just type, Enter, type, Enter.

The same panel sits at the top of the site and story trainers, and on every Site by Site page. There it starts on the site you’re training, or on the folder you were reading if you opened the trainer from a folder. The new classifier shows up trained in its section right away, and the stories behind the dialog are rescored before you even close it.

Where it applies

Applies to sets the scope: one site, a folder, or all of your sites. It’s a new picker rather than a plain dropdown, so it shows your custom folder icons and each site’s favicon, and it has a search box at the top. With a few hundred subscriptions, typing three letters beats scrolling. While you search, nested folders show the folder they live in, so two folders called “Podcasts” don’t look identical.

The rules are the same as everywhere else in the trainer. A single site works on every account. Folders and all sites need Premium Archive, and so do text classifiers. URL classifiers need Premium, and regex needs Premium Pro. If you pick something your account doesn’t include, the panel tells you and links to the upgrade instead of letting you save a classifier that won’t do anything.

Regex

Title, author, text, and URL classifiers can be regular expressions. Click the .* at the end of the field to turn it on. The field gets a purple outline and a REGEX badge, the text switches to monospace, and the placeholder changes to an example for that type, so you always know which mode you’re in. Hover the .* and the same regex cheat sheet from the story trainer opens right there. A pattern that doesn’t compile is caught before it can be saved.

Super Dislike is now Hide

The third training level has been called Super Dislike since it launched, and I never loved the name. It says how strongly you feel, not what it does. What it does is hide the story, every time, even when the story also matches something you like. So it’s called Hide now, everywhere: on the web, on iOS and Mac, and on Android. Nothing about how it works has changed, and every super dislike you already have is a Hide.

If you ever forget how the three fit together, there’s an ⓘ next to them in the panel that lays it out with a couple of examples.

The same picker, everywhere

Once the scope picker existed, the plain folder dropdowns all over NewsBlur looked pretty sad next to it. So every folder chooser and every folder and site chooser on the web uses it now: adding a site, Add + Discover, the statistics, site settings, and notifications dialogs, Organize Sites, the default folder in Preferences, dashboard rivers, and the Daily Briefing. They all get the icons, the search, and the keyboard. Arrow keys, Enter, and Escape work the way you’d expect, or just start typing.

A few fixes along the way

  • Back to trainer from a matching stories list now takes you back to exactly where you were: the same tab, the same filters, any changes you hadn’t saved yet, and scrolled to the same classifier. It used to drop you on Site by Site every time.
  • The View matching stories button sits next to the classifier it belongs to instead of leaning toward the next one, and its tooltip no longer hangs around after you click it.
  • In the matching stories banner, Back to trainer no longer squeezes the Train and Notify on controls on a narrow story list.
  • Jump to folder in Organize Sites actually jumps to the folder.

Availability

Typing classifiers into Manage Training and the new folder and site picker are available now on the web. Hide is on the web now and comes to iOS, Mac, and Android with their next updates. Thanks to the forum for the nudge on this one. If there’s a classifier you want to type in that the panel can’t handle yet, let me know on the NewsBlur forum.

entry.title: Listen: NewsBlur reads your stories aloud on the web, iOS, Mac, and Android

link.title: Listen: NewsBlur reads your stories aloud on the web, iOS, Mac, and Android

entry.content:
Every story in NewsBlur now has a Listen button. Press it and NewsBlur reads the story to you, starting with the headline and going paragraph by paragraph, highlighting each one as it goes. When the story ends, the next one starts. It works on the web, iPhone, iPad, Mac, and Android starting today, and it can read stories in all 21 languages NewsBlur speaks.

Here’s Jon, the default English voice, reading that paragraph:

And if you’re reading this in NewsBlur, you can press Listen right now and have the rest of this post read to you.

This one launched everywhere on the same day. The web, the iOS and Mac apps, and the Android app all got Listen together, with its interface translated into the same 21 languages from last week’s language launch. If you already play podcasts in NewsBlur’s media player, Listen turns any story into one more thing to queue up.

Press Listen

On the web, Listen sits with the other story buttons, and the y key does the same thing. On iPhone, iPad, and Android it’s in the row of buttons at the end of each story. On the Mac it’s in the Story menu, also on Y, with a play and pause button in the toolbar.

On the web, stories play in the sidebar, in the same mini player that handles podcasts and YouTube. On iPhone, iPad, and Android, a mini player sits above the bottom bar. Tap it to open Now Playing, with a scrubber, 15 seconds back, 30 seconds forward, speed, and a button to skip to the next story.

Follow along

While a story plays, the paragraph being read is highlighted and the story scrolls gently to keep it in view. If you scroll away to look at something, it waits a few seconds before following again. Click or tap any paragraph to jump straight to it, which is also the quickest way past a long intro.

Listen reads the headline, then the article’s paragraphs, headings, lists, and quotes. It skips what doesn’t work out loud: images, captions, code blocks, tables, and embeds. And if a feed only publishes a summary, Listen fetches the full article from the site and reads that, so you hear the whole story and not just the first two sentences.

Up Next

Next to Listen is a small + that adds the story to Up Next. Queue a few stories while you read, press play, and walk away. Drag to reorder, and swipe or tap × to remove one.

When Up Next runs out, Listen keeps going with the next unread stories in whatever feed or folder you’re in. Each story is marked read when it finishes, and the reader follows along to the next one. If you’d rather it stop after each story, turn off Auto-continue.

Up Next is the same queue your podcasts use, and it’s saved to your account. Queue a story on your phone and it’s waiting in Up Next on the web.

Pick a voice

The voices come from ElevenLabs. Each language has ten recommended voices, and you can search the rest of the ElevenLabs library by gender, age, accent, and style. Every voice has a play button so you can hear it before you choose.

Delivery sets how much emotion goes into the reading: Steady, Natural, or Expressive. Fine-tune voice opens up the stability, similarity, and style settings behind those three if you want to tinker.

Speed goes from 0.5× to 3×, with presets and a slider for anything in between. The pitch stays put at any speed, so 1.5× sounds like a fast talker and not a chipmunk.

Every language gets its own voice

Listen works out what language each story is written in and reads it with your voice for that language. Jon reads my English stories, and when a French story comes through, Victoria picks it up. Choose a different voice for any language from the menu at the top of the voice list. These are the defaults:

Keeps playing with the screen off

On iPhone, iPad, and Android, Listen keeps going when you lock your phone or switch apps. It shows up on the lock screen, in Control Center, and in Android’s media controls, with the same 15 and 30 second skips, and headphone buttons play and pause.

On the Mac

The Mac app has Listen and Add to Up Next in the Story menu, and a play and pause button in the toolbar so you can stop a story without hunting for the player. Now Playing opens as a sheet over the reader, with the same Up Next list as everywhere else.

Try it for 30 seconds

Listen is part of Premium Archive and Premium Pro. On a free or Premium account you can still try it: Listen plays a 30 second preview of a few stories a day. Voice previews in the picker work too, so you can find a voice you like first.

How it works

Reading every story in everyone’s feeds ahead of time would be a huge waste, so Listen makes the audio on demand. When you press play, NewsBlur splits the story into short segments, usually a paragraph each, and asks ElevenLabs for the first one. The audio streams to you while it’s still being generated, so it starts quickly, and the next segment is fetched while the current one plays. Each segment is sent along with the text around it so the voice keeps its rhythm across paragraph breaks.

Once a segment has been read in a voice, it’s saved. The next person who listens to that story with the same voice gets it right away, and if you stop halfway through a story, the rest of it never gets made at all.

Availability

Listen is available today on the web, in NewsBlur for iPhone, iPad, and Mac on the App Store, and in NewsBlur for Android on Google Play. If you don’t want the button, you can hide it, along with any other story button, in Preferences on the web and in the apps, and that choice syncs between them.

I’d love to hear which voice you picked and how Listen handles your feeds. Let me know on the NewsBlur forum.

entry.title: A folder picker with room for every folder

link.title: A folder picker with room for every folder

entry.content:
When you right click a site and choose Change folders, NewsBlur shows a list of your folders. For years that list was a tiny box about four rows tall, no matter how big your screen was. A reader on the forum who files a lot of newsletters wrote up what was wrong with it: the box was too small, it ignored the custom folder icons they use to find things at a glance, and checking a new folder added the site there instead of moving it. They were right on all three, so I rebuilt it.

The list now grows to show every folder you have, as many as your window has room for, with the same icons you see in your sidebar. It opens scrolled to the folder the site is in now, and the text follows your sidebar’s text size.

Click a folder’s name and the site moves there. The old folder unchecks itself, and the button at the top reads Move to Tech, so you know exactly what’s about to happen. If you keep a site in more than one folder, click the circles beside the folders instead. Each circle adds or removes just that folder, and the button reads Save 2 folders.

Type to find a folder

There’s a filter box at the top of the picker, ready for typing as soon as it opens. Type a few letters and the list narrows to the folders that match, with their parent folders kept in place. The arrow keys move between matches, Enter picks one, and Enter again moves the site. So moving a site from Newsletters into Cooking can be a right click, a few letters, and two presses of Enter.

The new folder picker is available now on the web. If something about it doesn’t feel right, let me know on the NewsBlur forum.

entry.title: NewsBlur 16 for Mac: your dashboard in widgets, your news in notifications

link.title: NewsBlur 16 for Mac: your dashboard in widgets, your news in notifications

entry.content:
On the web, I keep NewsBlur’s dashboard open all day with a few folders side by side, so I can glance over and see what’s new. On my Mac I wanted that same glance without a browser tab or the app sitting in front of me. NewsBlur 16 for Mac gets there with two pieces that work together: widgets that each show a folder or site of your choice, and native Mac notifications from the sites you pick.

Put together, they give you a way to follow the news while you work. Headlines from the folders you care about sit one swipe away, and new stories from the handful of sites you never want to miss show up in the corner of your screen. You don’t have to pick up your phone to check, and you don’t have to open a reader and lose twenty minutes in it.

A dashboard made of widgets

Every NewsBlur widget now has its own source. Add one for All Site Stories, another for your Tech folder, and another for a single site you follow closely. Each one shows its own newest unread stories. Stack them in Notification Center or put them on your desktop, and you’ve got the NewsBlur dashboard living right in macOS.

Widgets come in two sizes. Medium shows three stories and large shows six. They follow your training, so stories you’ve trained away stay out of them. Click a story and it opens right in the Mac app.

Setting up a widget

Click the date and time in the menu bar to open Notification Center, then click Edit Widgets at the bottom. Search for NewsBlur, pick a size, and add it. If you’d rather have it on your desktop, right click the desktop and choose Edit Widgets instead.

New widgets start with All Site Stories. To change that, right click the widget, choose Edit Widget, and pick a folder or site. Folders are listed first, then every site you subscribe to, and there’s a search field if your list is long. Each widget keeps its own choice, so you can add as many as you want.

If you already had a NewsBlur widget, remove it and add it again to get the new version.

Notifications from the sites you pick

Widgets are for glancing. Notifications are for the stories you don’t want to wait on. NewsBlur can send a native Mac notification for new stories on any site, and clicking one takes you straight to that story in the app.

To turn them on, open a site and choose Site > Notifications… from the menu bar. Pick whether you want every unread story or only Focus stories, and turn on iOS, which covers both your iPhone and the Mac app. File > Notifications (Command Shift N) lists every site you’ve set up, so you can adjust them all in one place.

Focus is what keeps this from getting noisy. If you’ve trained a site, only the stories you like will reach you. And if a busy site only matters when it mentions a certain topic or author, per-classifier notifications let you get pinged for just those stories. Those are available on Premium Archive and Premium Pro.

The workflow

Here’s a setup that works well. Put a large widget at the top of Notification Center for the folder you read most, and a couple of medium widgets below it for folders you check less often. Turn on notifications for only the few sites where timing matters, set to Focus. Then get back to work.

When you want a break, swipe in from the right edge of your trackpad with two fingers and the whole dashboard is there. When something you care about is published, it comes to you. Either way your phone stays face down on the desk.

Everything else in NewsBlur 16 for Mac

  • NewsBlur for Mac now speaks 21 languages. Choose one from the NewsBlur menu, or follow your Mac’s language settings. Arabic and Hebrew read right to left, and your stories stay exactly as published. More about that in NewsBlur in your language.
  • Clicking a story slides to it in the right direction.
  • The sidebar has more balanced spacing and compact filters, with Add Site and Settings kept separate.
  • Command W closes the window while NewsBlur keeps running. Click the Dock icon to bring it back, or press Command Q to quit.
  • Keyboard shortcuts work while the story list has focus, and N opens the first unread story.
  • Space pages down through a story, and when you reach the bottom it opens the next unread story, just like on the web. Shift Space pages back up and opens the previous story at the top. You can set how far each press scrolls in Preferences or in the Keyboard Shortcuts dialog.

NewsBlur 16 is available now on the Mac App Store. If you’ve found a widget setup you like, or something isn’t working the way you’d expect, I’d love to hear about it on the NewsBlur forum.

entry.title: NewsBlur in your language: native language support on the web, iOS, and Android

link.title: NewsBlur in your language: native language support on the web, iOS, and Android

entry.content:
Since 2009, NewsBlur has only spoken English. Plenty of you read feeds in other languages every day, and you’ve still had to find your way around the reader in English. Starting today, NewsBlur’s interface is available in 21 languages on the web, iOS, and Android. Menus, buttons, settings, dialogs, and the first-time setup all appear in your language, picked up automatically from your browser or phone.

Your stories stay exactly as they were published. NewsBlur translates its own interface, not the feeds you read. Feed titles, story text, comments, and usernames all stay in their original language. The screenshot above is NewsBlur in Japanese, reading an English article from Ars Technica.

Picked up automatically

You don’t need to do anything to switch. On the web, NewsBlur uses your browser’s language. On iOS and Android, it uses your phone’s language list. If your language isn’t one of the 21, everything stays in English.

Because a new language can be a surprise, NewsBlur tells you which one it picked the first time you open it. The dialog shows the same message side by side, in the language it detected and in English. One button keeps it, the other switches back to English. That way you can always get back, even if NewsBlur guessed wrong because you’re traveling, living abroad, or using a VPN.

If NewsBlur picked English, you’ll see a shorter version with every language listed in its own script, in case you’d rather read in another one. New accounts get the same choice as the very first step of setup.

Choose your language on the web

You can change your language anytime in Preferences, right at the top under Language. Automatic follows your browser, or you can pick any language. If you’re signed out, there’s a language menu at the top of the home page, so the sign in and sign up forms are in your language before you even have an account.

Choose your language on iOS

On iPhone and iPad, open Preferences and choose Language at the top. Pick a language and the app switches right away, no restart needed.

Everything follows along, from your feed list to the story controls.

Choose your language on Android

On Android, it’s the first row in Settings. The app switches as soon as you choose, and Android also lets you set NewsBlur’s language from the system’s per-app language settings.

Menus and numbers follow your language too.

One language, everywhere you read

When you pick a language, it’s saved to your account, so your phone and the web stay in sync. If you leave it on Automatic, each device follows its own language settings. That’s handy if your laptop is in English and your phone is in Spanish.

Here are all 21 languages:

  • English
  • Español
  • Français
  • Deutsch
  • Português (Brasil)
  • Italiano
  • Nederlands
  • Polski
  • Türkçe
  • Русский
  • Українська
  • العربية
  • עברית
  • हिन्दी
  • Bahasa Indonesia
  • Tiếng Việt
  • ไทย
  • 日本語
  • 한국어
  • 简体中文
  • 繁體中文

Arabic and Hebrew switch the whole interface to read right to left.

Help me get the words right

If you read NewsBlur in one of these languages, I’d love your help. If a button reads awkwardly, a term sounds wrong, or a phrase doesn’t fit, tell me on the NewsBlur forum. Mention the language, where you saw it, and what it should say, and I’ll get it fixed.

Native language support is available now on the web and coming in the next iOS and Android updates.

entry.title: A new first-time experience on iOS and Android: find your first feeds

link.title: A new first-time experience on iOS and Android: find your first feeds

entry.content:
An empty reader is a hard place to start. If you already know which sites you want to follow, adding them is straightforward. But if you’re trying RSS for the first time, finding those first few feeds is part of the work. I wanted NewsBlur to help with that, right inside the app.

I’ve rebuilt the first-time experience on iOS and Android around exploring interests, previewing feeds, and choosing what goes into your reader. You can put together a few folders of things you care about, or bring your existing collection from another app with an OPML import.

Explore your interests on iOS

After creating your account, the iPhone and iPad apps open a setup screen with Explore interests. Browse categories such as science, books, cooking, and technology, or search for a topic. A little of everything gives you a starting point if you’d rather sample a mix.

Each category opens a bundle of feeds. You can see what the sites actually publish through recent story previews, rather than choosing from names alone. Deselect feeds you don’t want, give the folder a name, and add the ones you like.

You can keep exploring and add another bundle before heading into the reader. The idea is to make those first subscriptions your own, with enough context to decide whether a feed belongs in your daily reading.

Build your first folders on Android

Android gets the same interest-based setup. Browse or search the catalog, open a bundle, and look through its feeds before subscribing. The import option is right at the top if you’re coming from another reader.

Feed cards show recent stories, how often a site publishes, and when it last updated. Choose the feeds you want and name the folder they’ll go into. A science folder, a cooking folder, and a handful of personal blogs can give you plenty to read without having to assemble every subscription one at a time.

The final setup step shows what you’ve added. Tap Start reading to head into your reader with your folders ready.

Bring your feeds, or come back for more

On both platforms, Import OPML brings your feeds and folders from another reader. Export an OPML file from your old app, save it somewhere your phone can access, and select it during setup.

You don’t need a new account to use the bundles. Existing readers can open Import or upload sites from the iOS menu or Import and feed bundles from the Android menu. It’s a way to explore a new interest whenever you want to add something to your reading.

The new setup experience is coming in the next iOS and Android updates, alongside Sign in with Apple and Google. I’d love to hear how the first few minutes feel, whether you’re starting fresh or helping someone else get into RSS. Let me know on the NewsBlur forum.

entry.title: Sign in with Apple or Google on the web, iOS, and Android

link.title: Sign in with Apple or Google on the web, iOS, and Android

entry.content:
NewsBlur has asked for a username and password since the beginning. That still works, but I wanted getting into your reader to be easier, especially on a new phone. I’ve added Sign in with Apple and Sign in with Google on the web, iOS, and Android. You can use either to create an account or connect to the NewsBlur account you already have.

Apple and Google sign-in on the web

The welcome page, login page, and signup page now have Apple and Google buttons above the usual username and password fields. Choose either provider to sign in or create a NewsBlur account. For a new account, you’ll choose a NewsBlur username so you still have your own name when sharing stories and commenting.

If you already have a NewsBlur account, you can connect it instead of starting over. Choose Connect an existing account and enter your NewsBlur username and password. If you try to create an account with a username that’s already taken, NewsBlur brings you to that connection step and explains what to do.

You only need to confirm your NewsBlur password when making that connection. Afterward, the Apple or Google button takes you back to the same feeds, saved stories, and subscription.

Different email addresses, one NewsBlur account

Your Apple email doesn’t have to match your Google email, and neither has to match your NewsBlur email. You can connect a personal Apple account and a work Google account to the same NewsBlur username. Connecting them leaves your NewsBlur email address unchanged.

Open Manage > Account on the web and look under your email address. The new Connected accounts section lists each connected Apple or Google account and its email. Use Connect Apple or Connect Google to add another, or the little × beside a connection to remove it.

An Apple or Google account can belong to one NewsBlur account at a time. To move it, disconnect it from the old account first. NewsBlur also makes sure you keep a way to sign in before removing your last connection.

Sign in on iOS

The iPhone and iPad apps get the same Apple and Google sign-in choices. You can also create an account with an email, username, and password right on the welcome screen.

Sign in on Android

Android gets both provider buttons as well, including Sign in with Apple. The account connection works across platforms: connect a provider on the web and use it to sign into that same NewsBlur account on your phone.

For new readers, both mobile apps also have a new first-time experience that helps you choose your first feeds and get reading.

Apple and Google sign-in are available now on the web and coming in the next iOS and Android updates. If you have feedback, let me know on the NewsBlur forum.

entry.title: NewsBlur 15 for Android: faster scrolling, a tablet layout, and Add + Discover Sites

link.title: NewsBlur 15 for Android: faster scrolling, a tablet layout, and Add + Discover Sites

entry.content:
I spent a lot of this release optimizing speed in the Android app. I measured scrolling across the feed list, the story list, and long articles, then fixed whatever the numbers pointed at. Then I kept going.

It’s faster

Most of the slowness came from the app doing more work than it needed to. Marking a story read rebuilt its entire row. Background syncs could pile up on top of each other. The feed list waited on the sync service before showing anything, and the reader waited for the article to finish rendering before it appeared at all.

All of that is fixed. Janky frames while scrolling the feed list dropped from 32% to 15%, and from 14% to 7% in the story list. Opening a story you’ve read before went from 0.9s to 0.2s. Your feeds now load straight from the local cache, so they show up right away, even offline.

Controls that float

The story list controls now float at the bottom of the screen, so your stories scroll right behind them. Search, display options, and settings are all within reach of your thumb. If you’d rather have them at the top, there’s a setting for that in Preferences. In the reader, the controls tuck away as you scroll down and come back as soon as you scroll up.

Built for tablets

On a tablet or an unfolded foldable, NewsBlur now shows your story list and the story you’re reading side by side. Your feeds slide in over the top when you need them and slide back out when you pick one, and the list stays right where it is while the new stories fill in. Tap another story and the reader pages over to it, the same way it does when you swipe. It works in both portrait and landscape.

A better look at images

Tap any image in a story to open it full screen. Pinch or double tap to zoom, and swipe it away to go right back to the story.

Long press an image and you get the same viewer with a little more. The image’s hover text shows up above it, which is where comics like xkcd keep the punchline. Below it are Copy Image, Save Image, and Share Image. Saving keeps the original file, so a GIF stays animated, and it lands in your Pictures folder. If the image is a link, there’s an Open Link button too.

Find your next favorite site

The + button opens a small Add Site sheet. Paste an address and pick a folder, or tap one of the shortcuts into discovery: Web Feed, Popular, Trending, YouTube, Reddit, Newsletters, Podcasts, and Google News. It’s the same Add + Discover Sites catalog from the web, built right into the app. Web Feed can even turn a site without RSS into a feed.

Every site shows its latest stories with images and excerpts, along with how recently it published. Tap a story to read it, or tap Try to browse the whole site before you subscribe. When you come back, discovery is right where you left it. Related Sites uses the same cards, so you can explore outward from a site you already like.

Everything else

  • Gestures are configurable. In Preferences you can choose what swiping left and right does on feeds and on stories, and what a long press does.
  • Long press a feed or a story for a grouped menu that includes Mark newer as read and Mark older as read.
  • Nested folders show up as an indented tree.
  • The Previous button no longer gets stuck disabled.
  • Jumping to the next folder no longer loops forever when nothing is unread.

NewsBlur 15 for Android is available on Google Play. The iOS and Mac release got a lot of the same work. If something doesn’t feel right, let me know on the NewsBlur forum.

entry.title: NewsBlur 15 for iOS and Mac: faster story lists, a glass toolbar, and Add + Discover Sites

link.title: NewsBlur 15 for iOS and Mac: faster story lists, a glass toolbar, and Add + Discover Sites

entry.content:
I spent a lot of this release optimizing speed in the iOS app. Opening a big folder took over a second, scrolling would hitch whenever the next page of stories loaded, and articles flashed blank for a moment before appearing. So I measured every part of the story list and the reader, then fixed whatever the numbers pointed at.

Faster story lists

Loading the next page of a folder used to reload the entire list. Now new stories are added in place. Favicons, thumbnails, and story text get prepared in the background ahead of time instead of while you’re scrolling. Opening a feed shows its cached stories immediately while fresh ones load, and articles appear fully laid out instead of flashing blank first.

Opening All Site Stories went from 1.1s to 0.2s. A single feed went from 0.7s to 0.2s. Loading another page into a list of 5,000 stories went from 0.7s to 0.02s.

A glass toolbar

The story list toolbar is now a floating glass bar at the bottom of the screen on iPhone and iPad, and your stories scroll right behind it. Related Sites, story order, and search are on the left. Add and Mark as read are on the right. If you’d rather keep it at the top, you can move it back in Preferences. In the reader, the controls hide as you scroll down and come back when you scroll up.

Images

Tap an image in a story and it opens full screen, zooming out from its spot in the article. Pinch or double tap to zoom, drag to look around, and swipe to go back. On iPad the viewer covers all three columns, and you land right back where you were in the story.

Long press an image to see its hover text above it, which is where comics like xkcd hide the punchline. Copy Image, Save Image, and Share Image are right there with it.

Add + Discover Sites

The + button opens a Quick Add sheet. Paste an address or search for a site, pick a folder, and add it. Below that are shortcuts into every discovery source: Search, Web Feed, Popular, YouTube, Reddit, Newsletters, Podcasts, and Google News. You can swipe between them like pages. It’s the same Add + Discover Sites catalog from the web, rebuilt natively for iOS.

Each site shows its latest stories with an image and a short excerpt, along with how recently it published. Tap a story to read it, or tap Try to browse the site without subscribing. When you come back, you’re in the same spot with that story highlighted. On iPad, Try keeps all three columns, so you can browse a new site and read its stories side by side. Related Sites uses the same cards.

Offline storage that cleans up after itself

A reader on the forum noticed NewsBlur using 4.2 GB on their iPhone with no unread stories. Digging in turned up three bugs in the offline cache. Cleanup skipped pruning whenever you were all caught up, it never cleared cached article text, and it compacted the database before deleting anything, so no space ever came back.

All three are fixed. Cleanup now keeps storage within your Stories to store limit, and Delete offline stories in Preferences actually gives you the space back. Your subscriptions and any pending read or save changes are kept.

Everything else

  • Long press any feed, folder, or story for a native menu.
  • Mark newer as read and Mark older as read update your unread counts right away, even inside collapsed folders and while offline.
  • Feed and story gestures each have their own settings.
  • The Mac app gets the new discovery screen, image viewer, menus, and offline cleanup too.
  • Tapping a notification opens the story instead of sometimes getting stuck.
  • Reading positions are restored correctly.

NewsBlur 15 is available on the App Store for iPhone, iPad, and Mac. The Android release got a lot of the same work. If you have feedback, I’d love to hear it on the NewsBlur forum.

entry.title: Matching Stories: see every story behind a tag, author, or classifier

link.title: Matching Stories: see every story behind a tag, author, or classifier

entry.content:
The Intelligence Trainer has always asked you to decide blind. You see a tag or an author on a story and you can train it up or down, but you can’t see what else that decision would touch. Is this author a regular on this site or a one-time guest? Does the “review” tag mean product reviews or book reviews? How many stories does “sponsored” actually hit? Until now the only way to find out was to train it and watch the scores change across the feed.

Now every tag, author, and URL on a story has a small button next to it: View matching stories. Click it and the story list turns into a view of every story on that site that carries that exact value. Not just unread stories, read ones too, so you get the whole picture. It’s the fastest way I’ve found to answer “what else is like this?”

From a story

Open any story and look at the author and tags under the title. Each one now has a small stories icon beside it. Click it and the list filters down to every story that matches that one author or tag. The URL line gets the same button, so you can pull up every story that shares a path segment, which turns out to be a great way to find a series or a podcast on a site that doesn’t tag its posts.

The matching text is highlighted on every row of the filtered list. An author filter marks the author on each story, a title filter marks the words it matched, and a text filter marks the phrase in the preview.

A URL filter is a little different, since the link isn’t normally part of the story list. When one is active, each row grows a URL line with the matched segment highlighted, so you can see exactly why the story is there.

The filter rides along in the URL, so reload, back and forward, and bookmarks all do what you’d expect. I have a few of these bookmarked now for authors I check in on every couple of weeks.

From the trainer

The same button lives in the Intelligence Trainer on every tag, author, title, URL, and text classifier you’ve saved. This is the part I’ve wanted for years. You trained “sponsored” as hidden a long time ago and have a nagging feeling it’s swallowing something it shouldn’t. Click the magnifying glass on that classifier, the trainer closes, and you’re looking at exactly the stories it hides. A Back to trainer link in the banner takes you back to where you were.

Regex classifiers and natural language classifiers don’t get the button, since neither one matches a single exact value.

The banner

At the top of every filtered list is a banner that names the filter and gives you three things to do with it.

Filter stories widens the list from this site to the whole folder or to all of your sites. Site scope is available to everyone. Folder and All follow the same rule as folder and global classifiers, so they need Premium Archive. On Archive, a folder or all-sites tag filter runs against the story search index rather than a window of recent stories, so a tag that appears on a dozen stories spread across forty sites turns up all twelve.

Train is Like, Dislike, or Hide (the super dislike). It saves the same classifier the trainer would, and the list recomputes in place: the score flips on each row, the unread counts in the sidebar update, and stories you just trained down stay in the list so you can see what you did instead of watching rows vanish out from under you.

Notify on is Email, Web, iOS, and Android. These are the per-classifier notifications from earlier this year, now reachable from the same banner. You find a tag, confirm it matches what you think it matches, and turn on a notification for it without ever opening the trainer.

One detail worth knowing: the Filter stories toggle only changes what you’re looking at. Training and notifications still write to the classifier’s own scope. Browsing a tag across a folder doesn’t quietly turn a site classifier into a folder classifier.

A few ways I’ve been using it

  • Deciding whether to follow an author. A group blog has a new writer. Click the button beside their name, read three of their stories, then Like them from the banner.
  • Auditing a hidden tag. Open the trainer, click the magnifying glass on a red tag, and check that it’s hiding what you meant it to hide.
  • Pulling up a series. Click the button on the URL line of a story with /podcast/ in the link and every episode on the site lines up.
  • Setting up a notification with confidence. Widen a tag to a folder, see that it matches the right kind of story, and turn on the iOS notification right there.

Availability

Matching Stories is available now on the web for everyone. Site scope, training, and highlighting work on every account. Folder and All scopes and the Notify on controls follow the existing rules for Premium Archive and Premium Pro.

If you find a tag or author that should match and doesn’t, or have an idea for where else this button belongs, let me know on the NewsBlur forum.
